title: OT/ICS Threat Intel - All Critical Infrastructure
description: Curated OT/ICS cybersecurity advisories, incidents and threat intelligence from primary sources. Editorial summaries by Mike Holcomb in partnership with UtilSec.

_otthreatfeed.usage: Free to reuse with attribution. Credit 'Mike Holcomb & UtilSec' and link back to otthreatfeed.com and to each item's linked primary source. Summaries are editorial paraphrase - verify against the primary source before acting.

items.title: Coast Guard confirms cyber boardings of US-bound ships as officials weigh Iran’s role in up to 50 tanker attacks
items.content_text: US officials told the Wall Street Journal, in a report carried on 23–24 November, that Iran is the main suspect in as many as 50 cyberattacks on tankers carrying oil, gas and chemicals; Russia is also being examined, and an administration official says there is no evidence of Iranian involvement. The Coast Guard and FBI have now confirmed boarding two foreign-flagged ships in the Gulf of Mexico on 21 and 24 August after signs their networks were compromised, and cyber teams have assisted at least four US-bound vessels, including the VL Prosperity, which received a ransom note and a bomb threat. Bloomberg reports that investigators found evidence hackers reached one supertanker’s propulsion system, which is not confirmed, and the suggested entry through Fortinet firewalls is unsettled. For OT defenders, vessel and terminal networks, and the edge devices that reach them, are now live targets.

items.title: CISA and FBI warn of an ongoing threat to internet-connected refrigeration as European supermarket attacks reach at least 11 countries
items.content_text: Hackers are tampering with internet-connected refrigeration controllers in European supermarkets; on 5 November CISA and the FBI, with HHS, USDA and DOT, warned the threat is ongoing and reaches healthcare, chemical, transport and cold-storage operations. Hundreds of French stores were hit in October; a second wave on 1–2 November reached about 11 countries, forcing units into continuous heating or defrost, and three French blood-service sites had settings changed with no blood lost. Sweden’s NCSC says victims at Coop and ICA stores mainly ran older systems from one manufacturer with weak passwords. Belgium’s interior minister said on 12 November that evidence points to Iran, short of formal attribution; the EU is preparing sanctions (see Trends). Sekoia says the second wave used a non-public, unauthenticated flaw that renames the controller’s admin account. If a controller is reachable from the internet, treat it as at risk today.

items.title: PHP2Shell attacks rooted about two dozen Palo Alto firewalls, and Siemens, Schneider and ABB now list grid-control, DCS and RTU products, several with no fix
items.content_text: Palo Alto’s Unit 42 verified that a suspected China-nexus actor chained the PHP2Shell flaws (CVE-2026-109618, CVE-2026-109619) with Linux kernel bug CVE-2026-46300 to root about two dozen internet-exposed PAN-OS firewalls on 23–24 October and steal Active Directory credentials. Siemens (Spectrum Power, AMIS TS and, since 16 November, WTV676/WTV776 metering gateways), Schneider (a Foxboro DCS server) and ABB (Netcontrol RTUs, ASPECT gateways) now list affected products, several unfixed. None is reported exploited and no OT operator is named: treat it as an IT-to-OT boundary warning.

items.title: A Chilean solar-and-battery plant is still off the grid nearly three months after a cyberattack, and lawmakers want answers
items.content_text: The 103 MW Huatacondo solar plant in Chile’s Tarapacá region, with a 98 MW / 312 MWh battery system in commissioning, has been off the national grid since the National Electric Coordinator triggered its disconnection protocol on 27 August after a reported cyberattack. Its 14 November report still lists both assets at zero availability. On 11 November a member of Congress asked whether the national cybersecurity agency was notified as the law requires and which control systems were hit; no answer by 16 November. The owner, entry route and affected systems are undisclosed. The lesson: a plant pulled off the grid for safety can stay dark for months if it cannot be restored with confidence (editorial assessment).

items.title: Norway says the Equinor and Skagerak intrusions came through Microsoft’s Azure API Management cloud service
items.content_text: On 23 November Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said an unidentified actor has been stealing access tokens and other sensitive data from Microsoft Azure API Management (APIM), and that Equinor and Skagerak Energi were among the organisations hit. Equinor detected its intrusion on 17 November and contained it by 20 November; Skagerak disclosed a separate attack a day later. Both say oil, gas and electricity production carried on normally, and Equinor sees no sign data was stolen or altered. A reported, non-public Microsoft notice says an issue in older “Classic” APIM tiers was found on 18 November and the access path closed the next day; Microsoft has issued credential-rotation guidance but has not publicly linked it to Norway. NSM found no service disruption. Operators using cloud APIs to move plant or market data should rotate those secrets now (editorial assessment).

items.title: Illinois investigates an apparent cyberattack attempt on the Algonquin Dam on the Fox River
items.content_text: The Illinois Department of Natural Resources said on 20 November that it detected an apparent attempted cyberattack on the Algonquin Dam, about 45 miles northwest of Chicago, on 16 November. Staff blocked the unauthorised access at once, and the dam stayed secure and fully operational. IDNR has not said which system was targeted or whether gate controls were reachable. Illinois State Police, state agencies and CISA are investigating; no link to other attacks and no group has been named. For dam and flood-control owners, it is a prompt to check who can reach gate and spillway controls remotely (editorial assessment).

items.title: Peninsula Energy shuts its Wyoming uranium plant and wellfield after a cyberattack reaches their control systems
items.content_text: Peninsula Energy said on 25 November that the incident its US subsidiary Strata Energy found on the morning of 20 November hit the plant and wellfield operating and control systems at its Lance in-situ uranium project in Crook County, Wyoming. Lance has been shut down and the affected systems isolated; corporate and administrative systems in the US and Australia, including payroll and finance, are unaffected. US authorities were notified and outside forensic advisers engaged. The company cannot yet say whether 2027 production guidance is at risk, and its shares are suspended until 30 November or a restart announcement. The entry route and attacker are undisclosed and no group has claimed it. A control-system hit that forces a full shutdown is the case a rehearsed safe-state plan exists for (editorial assessment).

items.title: South Korea’s state power utility KEPCO confirms about 1.5 million records stolen, as turbine maker Suzlon reports its own incident
items.content_text: Korea Electric Power Corp (KEPCO) confirmed on 22 November that an attacker got into its internal network and reached two systems: its KEPCO ON customer billing and payment platform and its supplier procurement system. It detected the intrusion on 20 November, cut external access and suspended the affected services. The company says data on about 650,000 customers, 427,000 supplier representatives and 443,000 employees was exposed, roughly 1.52 million people. It has not said how the attacker got in, and a forum actor’s 19 November claim is unverified. No effect on power supply is reported. A day later India’s Suzlon Energy disclosed a cyber incident and said business-critical applications were unaffected. Procurement systems hold supplier contacts and project details that make good phishing material for grid vendors (editorial assessment).

items.title: Ransomware halts smart-meter production and shipments at Japan’s Osaki Electric
items.content_text: Osaki Electric, a Japanese smart-meter maker, said ransomware encrypted data on its servers on 17 November, and it suspended production and shipments at its Saitama centre and at group companies Iwate Osaki Electric and Osaki Platech. The company believes the intruder got in on 15 November through a VPN device by guessing the password of an account without multi-factor authentication. In a 25 November update it confirmed data was sent from internal systems to an outside destination, said production equipment and meters already in customer use are unaffected, and set a tentative plan: staged production from 27 November, shipments of existing orders from 1 December and new orders from 7 December. No group has claimed it. For utilities the risk is supply-chain: delayed meter rollouts and how suppliers protect the systems that build and sign devices (editorial assessment).

items.title: Cyberattack on Brazil’s Santos port authority forces manual workarounds at Latin America’s busiest port
items.content_text: The Port of Santos authority, which runs Brazil’s largest port, lost its IT systems on 6 November and on 10 November confirmed a cyberattack. Access-control systems and digital tools for coordinating port operations went down, delaying vessel, truck and train procedures and forcing some checks, such as matching ship dimensions to berths, to be done by hand. The port’s protection level was raised to 2 of 3 on 8 November. By 16 November main internal systems were in final tests and about 70% of affected file backups were recovered; ship movements and landside access continued throughout. Brazil’s Federal Police are investigating; the attacker, entry route and any data theft are undisclosed. For port operators, access control and berth planning need a tested manual fallback (editorial assessment).

items.title: DHS tells Congress Iran-backed hackers have stepped up attacks on US water, energy and transport since February, while officials rule out hacking in last week’s outages
items.content_text: In written testimony for a House Homeland Security Committee hearing on 18 November, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Iranian state-sponsored groups and pro-Iranian criminals have targeted US critical infrastructure since the conflict with Iran began in February, with transportation, healthcare, water, energy and financial services increasingly in their sights. He described the attacks so far as mostly localized, low-damage disruptions of poorly secured industrial control systems, but warned that weak systems and poor cyber hygiene could have devastating consequences. At the same hearing the Director of National Intelligence and DHS said they found no evidence that hackers caused last week’s Microsoft 365 outage, the nationwide FAA ground stop or other recent disruptions, which officials tie to software defects and upgrade failures. Separately, AttackIQ research released on 17 November describes Iranian groups handing network access to one another, with long-running espionage access later passed to teams pursuing destructive goals, sometimes disguised as ransomware or hacktivism, often reaching targets through contractors and suppliers. For OT owners, the official US view now matches France’s: Iran is going after the weakest exposed controllers.

items.title: Dragos counts 1,266 ransomware attacks on industrial organizations in Q3, up 11%, and found no case of an operator touching a control system
items.content_text: Dragos said on 16 November that ransomware hit 1,266 industrial organizations between July and September 2026, up 11% on the second quarter, while the number of brands claiming industrial victims jumped from 70 to 99. Manufacturing took 69% of cases, followed by the ICS ecosystem of integrators, engineering firms and equipment makers (116) and transport and logistics (105); oil and gas logged 47. Qilin and The Gentlemen drove 29% of the total. Dragos saw no Q3 case of a ransomware operator manipulating a control system: production stopped because the IT, ERP and virtualization layers plants rely on went down, as when Fairlife reportedly halted all four of its US plants for about 11 days. Entry came through edge devices and enterprise applications exploited within days of disclosure, and through stolen VPN and firewall credentials. Check Point separately counted a record 1,063 claimed victims across all sectors in October.

items.title: GreyNoise says an AI-assisted crew breached Check Point firewall-management servers at 22 organizations, including energy, transport and manufacturing firms
items.content_text: GreyNoise reported on 24 November a campaign it tracks as GT13 that compromised Check Point Security Management servers at at least 22 organizations in several countries between 17 October and 2 November; it lost visibility after that and believes attempts continue. Victims include energy, transportation, mining, engineering and manufacturing firms. The attackers used a Rejetto HFS file server as a relay, then CVE-2026-16232 in SmartConsole to run scripts on management servers, copying firewall databases and internal certificate authorities and unloading security policies. GreyNoise believes AI tools did much of the work with human operators involved, and cannot name the group or country; Check Point says no new vulnerability or technique is involved. A firewall manager holds the rulebook for the IT/OT boundary, so a stolen policy database is a map of the plant perimeter (editorial assessment).

items.title: A vCenter authentication bypass was exploited as a zero-day for two months before Broadcom’s 19 November patch; vCenter 7.0 gets no fix
items.content_text: Broadcom patched CVE-2026-123890 on 19 November, a critical flaw in vCenter’s directory service that lets a remote, unauthenticated attacker obtain an administrator session. Google’s Mandiant, which reported the bug, says a suspected China-linked espionage group it tracks as Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221, also called Warp Panda) exploited it for more than two months beforehand. In the incidents Mandiant investigated, the group got in through a BeyondTrust Remote Support flaw, moved to Linux appliances, attacked vCenter in early September with a custom tool called Bonesaw, stole SAML signing material and the vCenter master key, created an SSO admin account, forged tokens and moved on to ESXi hosts. Fixes are in vCenter 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m; end-of-life vCenter 7.0 has no public patch. No victims or sectors are named. Many plants run HMIs, historians and engineering workstations as virtual machines, so whoever controls vCenter controls those hosts (editorial assessment).

items.title: Danfoss assigns two critical CVEs to its refrigeration system managers, confirms firmware 5.4.0 is affected, and says the fix will not come until 5.5.x
items.content_text: Danfoss published two security advisories on 20 November that put CVE numbers on the refrigeration-controller weaknesses behind this month’s European warnings. CVE-2026-129713 (CVSS v4 9.3) is a stack buffer overflow in an unauthenticated web handler of AK-SM 8xxA system managers, the store-level controllers that run supermarket and cold-storage refrigeration, up to and including firmware 5.4.0, which settles the earlier dispute over whether 5.4.0 was safe. Danfoss says the fix will come in the upcoming 5.5.x release, which will also remove the option to switch Strict mode off. CVE-2026-127057 (CVSS v4 9.9) covers default credentials documented in the manuals of legacy AK-SC 355 and AK-SM 800 units, all versions. The advisories follow Midnight Blue’s disclosure of six pre-login overflows and warnings from Belgium’s CCB, Germany’s BSI and Ireland’s NCSC. Neither CVE is reported as exploited or listed in CISA KEV. Until 5.5.x ships, keeping these units off the internet is the real control.

items.title: A Brotli flaw already in CISA’s exploited list turns up in Siemens WinCC, WinCC OA and BRAUMAT, and most products have no fix yet
items.content_text: Siemens says a widely used compression library flaw, CVE-2026-111497, reaches into several of its industrial software lines, and CISA republished the assessment as an ICS advisory on 17 November. The bug is an out-of-bounds write in the Brotli decoder that can crash the software, leak information or possibly allow code execution. CISA added the CVE to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on 27 October because of attacks elsewhere; nobody has reported exploitation through a Siemens product. Affected products named include BRAUMAT and SISTAR V8.2, WinCC OA V3.20 and V3.21, WinCC Runtime Professional, WinCC V7/V8 and TIA Administrator. Fixes exist only for BRAUMAT/SISTAR (V8.2 Update 5) and WinCC OA V3.20 (P17.1), so most sites must rely on the workaround for now (editorial assessment).

items.title: Java4Shell exploitation attempts begin, and Siemens tells customers to take Industrial Edge Management offline until patched
items.content_text: Probing for Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption bug in how OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later decode Base64 data, started within two days of its 17 November disclosure. GreyNoise counted more than 150 matching requests from five addresses by early 19 November and Previdian logged nine attempts from six addresses; none is confirmed to have succeeded. Exploitation needs a recent Intel or AMD x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, and researchers at Calif showed unauthenticated code execution against default Jira, Confluence, Jenkins and Keycloak setups, each with a tailored chain. For OT teams the key item is Siemens advisory SSA-272816: three Industrial Edge Management products are affected, fixes are in progress, and Siemens recommends taking those instances offline until they are patched. Cisco lists more than a dozen products with no fix yet, and Atlassian Data Center products are also unpatched.

items.title: Comments close 30 November on NIST’s draft rewrite of its OT security guide, which adds water, food, rail, maritime and building-automation coverage
items.content_text: NIST’s draft Revision 4 of SP 800-82, the US government’s main guide to operational technology security, is open for public comment until 30 November 2026. The draft reorganises the guide around Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, with risk management now led by the Govern function, and adds sector material for building automation, water and wastewater, food and agriculture, freight rail, maritime vessels, and industrial IoT connected to cloud services. It also expands guidance on asset management, network monitoring and detection, protecting system-management functions, and applying zero-trust principles. Many regulators, insurers and auditors use 800-82 as a reference, so its final wording can shape what operators are asked to show; the comment window is the chance for practitioners to flag guidance that would not work on a plant floor.
